name: Martin Bucer
role: Former Dominican friar, reformer of Strasbourg, Regius Professor of Divinity at Cambridge
summary: Reformer of Strasbourg who worked for unity among Protestants and with Catholics, mentored John Calvin, and ended his life in English exile. Under Mary I his body was dug up and burned as a heretic.

key_dates.label: Enters the Dominican order at Sélestat
Hears Luther at the Heidelberg Disputation and is won over
Released from his vows; marries the former nun Elisabeth Silbereisen
Takes part in the Marburg Colloquy between Luther and Zwingli
Negotiates the Wittenberg Concord with Luther on the Lord's Supper
Takes part in the Regensburg colloquy with Catholic theologians
Forced out of Strasbourg; becomes Regius Professor of Divinity at Cambridge

accomplishments.text: Led the Reformation in Strasbourg for a quarter-century, building a church order, schools, and care for the poor that influenced Reformed churches widely.
Worked tirelessly for agreement between the Lutheran and Swiss Reformations on the Lord's Supper, achieving the Wittenberg Concord with Luther (1536).
Co-wrote the Tetrapolitan Confession (1530) for Strasbourg and three other cities.
Hosted and mentored John Calvin in Strasbourg (1538–1541), whose later church order in Geneva drew on Bucer's model.
Took part in talks with Catholic theologians, including at Regensburg (1541), seeking reunion of the Western church.
With Luther and Melanchthon, gave secret approval in 1539 to the bigamous second marriage of Landgrave Philip of Hesse, which caused a scandal when it became known in 1540.
In England, wrote On the Kingdom of Christ (De Regno Christi, 1550) for Edward VI and a critique of the 1549 Prayer Book that influenced its 1552 revision.

persecution_note: Bucer was excommunicated by his bishop in 1523, forced out of Strasbourg by the emperor's religious settlement in 1549, and after his death in England was condemned as a heretic under Mary I, his body dug up and burned.

persecution.title: Excommunicated and driven out of Wissembourg
persecution.summary: As a married former friar preaching Reformation doctrine at Wissembourg (Weissenburg) in Alsace, Bucer was excommunicated by the Bishop of Speyer. He fled to Strasbourg, where, as the son of a citizen, he found protection.

responsible.name: Bishop of Speyer
responsible.role: Excommunicated him (George of the Palatinate, bishop 1513–1529)

defended_by.name: Strasbourg city council
defended_by.role: Allowed him to stay and later appointed him a preacher

persecution.outcome: He settled in Strasbourg, which became his base for 26 years.

persecution.title: Forced out of Strasbourg by the Augsburg Interim
persecution.summary: After defeating the Protestant princes, Emperor Charles V imposed the Augsburg Interim (1548), a religious settlement restoring much Catholic practice. Bucer refused to accept it, and the Strasbourg city council, under imperial pressure, dismissed him in March 1549.

defended_by.name: Thomas Cranmer
defended_by.role: Archbishop of Canterbury; invited him to England

persecution.outcome: He went to England, where Edward VI's government made him Regius Professor of Divinity at Cambridge.

persecution.title: Posthumous heresy trial; body exhumed and burned
persecution.summary: During Mary I's restoration of Catholicism, commissioners sent by Cardinal Reginald Pole to visit Cambridge University tried Bucer and the Hebrew scholar Paul Fagius for heresy after their deaths. Their bodies were dug up and burned on Market Hill in Cambridge on 6 February 1557, together with their books.

responsible.name: Cardinal Reginald Pole
responsible.role: Archbishop of Canterbury and papal legate; sent the visitors to Cambridge

responsible.name: Pole's visitors to Cambridge
responsible.role: Conducted the posthumous trial (led by Cuthbert Scott, Bishop of Chester)
responsible.jurisdiction: Legatine visitation of the University of Cambridge

responsible.name: Mary I
responsible.role: Queen of England, whose government restored the heresy laws

persecution.outcome: His remains were burned. Under Elizabeth I, the University of Cambridge formally restored his and Fagius's honor in 1560.

excommunication_note: Bucer was excommunicated by the Bishop of Speyer in 1523 and condemned as a heretic posthumously in 1557. The Catholic Church never lifted these sentences. The University of Cambridge publicly restored his honor in 1560 under Elizabeth I.

excommunications.reason: Married as a former friar and preached Reformation teaching at Wissembourg

excommunications.by: Cardinal Pole's legatine visitors to Cambridge
excommunications.reason: Condemned as a heretic; body exhumed and burned
excommunications.status: Reversed by the University of Cambridge under Elizabeth I (1560), not by Rome

sources.citation: Martin Bucer, De Regno Christi, in Melanchthon and Bucer, ed. Wilhelm Pauck, Library of Christian Classics 19 (Philadelphia: Westminster Press, 1969).
